outline.title: Abstract
outline.description: The abstract will provide a concise summary of the comprehensive survey on Large Language Model (LLM) security. It will highlight the rapid evolution of the threat landscape from 2023 to 2026, transitioning from basic, unimodal vulnerabilities to sophisticated, automated, and multimodal adversarial arms races. The abstract will briefly touch upon the four core threat categories: Data and Model Poisoning, Adversarial Attacks, Prompt Injection, and LLM Hallucinations. It will also summarize the paper's contributions, including the systematization of testing methodologies, the evaluation of cross-cutting defenses, and the identification of open challenges in securing foundation models.

outline.title: Introduction
outline.description: This section introduces the motivation, scope, and primary contributions of the survey. It contextualizes the explosive adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) across critical sectors, juxtaposed against the alarming expansion of their attack surface. The introduction will outline the chronological evolution of LLM security research from 2023 to 2026, noting the shift from identifying baseline vulnerabilities to navigating a highly sophisticated, co-evolutionary arms race between attackers and defenders. It will define the scope of the survey, explicitly covering training-time threats (data/model poisoning), inference-time threats (adversarial attacks, prompt injection), and output integrity issues (hallucinations). Finally, it will provide a roadmap of the paper, detailing how subsequent sections will systematically dissect threat vectors, testing methodologies, and mitigation strategies.

outline.title: Background and Preliminaries
outline.description: This section establishes the foundational concepts necessary for understanding LLM security. It will provide a brief overview of modern LLM and MLLM architectures, focusing on components that introduce security vulnerabilities, such as the pre-training corpus, alignment mechanisms like Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines. The section will formally define the threat model, distinguishing between white-box and black-box access, and categorizing adversaries based on their capabilities and objectives. It will also differentiate between training-time vulnerabilities (e.g., poisoning) and inference-time vulnerabilities (e.g., adversarial prompts, jailbreaks). By establishing this taxonomy, the section sets the stage for the detailed analysis of specific threat categories in the subsequent body sections.

outline.title: Training-Time Threats: Data and Model Poisoning
outline.description: This section explores the alarming evolution of data and model poisoning attacks from 2024 to 2025. It will detail the transition from unimodal text-based vulnerabilities to complex, multimodal, and embodied AI attack vectors. The discussion will begin with the foundational 2024 benchmarking studies by Chowdhury_2024_Breaking and Li_2024_Backdoorllm, which demonstrated how generative backdoors could be injected into open-source models like LLaMA-2, Mistral, and GPT-J, proving traditional defenses inadequate. The section will then analyze the late-2024/2025 turning point where attackers began exploiting specific alignment and retrieval mechanisms. A critical focus will be placed on the vulnerabilities of the Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) pipeline, illustrating how mechanisms traditionally viewed as safety alignments have been weaponized by sophisticated adversaries.

outline.title: Inference-Time Threats I: Adversarial Attacks
outline.description: This section examines the rapid evolution of adversarial attacks and defenses in LLMs and MLLMs between 2024 and 2026. It will highlight the transition from the identification of domain-specific vulnerabilities to a multi-faceted arms race. The section will specifically discuss 2024 research, such as Yang_2024_Adversarial, which exposed the alarming susceptibility of models deployed in critical sectors like healthcare, demonstrating manipulation using sensitive datasets like MIMIC-III. It will chronicle how early attacks focused on establishing baseline vulnerabilities before evolving into advanced offensive weaponization. The narrative will emphasize the shift in attack vectors, detailing how adversaries have moved beyond simple input perturbations to exploit the fundamental processing mechanics of both text-based and multimodal foundation models.

outline.title: Inference-Time Threats II: Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking
outline.description: Focusing on the 2025-2026 timeframe, this section details the transformative evolution of prompt injection and jailbreak attacks. It will document the definitive shift from static, rule-based bypasses to a highly dynamic, automated, and co-evolutionary adversarial landscape. The section will highlight how attackers successfully automated the discovery of adversarial prompts using adaptive optimization techniques. Specific attention will be given to the application of modified Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG), Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) fuzzing, and genetic algorithms, referencing the breakthrough works of Zhan_2025_LLM, Wang_2025_LLM, and Maloyan_2025_LLM. The discussion will emphasize how these automated techniques achieved alarming Attack Success Rates (ASR) ranging from 50% to 71% against state-of-the-art LLM agents in both black-box and agentic environments.

outline.title: Output Reliability and Integrity: LLM Hallucinations
outline.description: This section addresses the critical issue of LLM hallucinations and factual consistency, tracing its research evolution from 2023 to 2026. It will describe the shift from basic, computationally expensive detection mechanisms to highly optimized, mechanistically informed frameworks. The section will highlight the 2023 landmark development of zero-shot inference-time methods, specifically detailing the introduction of ChainPoll by Friel_2023_LLM. It will explain how ChainPoll demonstrated that LLM-based polling and Chain-of-Thought prompting could drastically reduce inference costs while outperforming contemporary competitors, establishing the paradigm of LLMs policing themselves. Furthermore, the section will explore the conceptual maturation that occurred in 2024, where the field moved away from treating all non-factual generations as binary errors, adopting more nuanced, conceptually rigorous approaches to factual consistency.

outline.title: Cross-Cutting Defenses and Mitigation Strategies
outline.description: This section synthesizes the holistic defense mechanisms developed to secure LLMs against the diverse threat vectors discussed previously. It traces the evolution of defenses from the 2024 'patchwork' approach to modern, integrated systems. The discussion will highlight early external stateful detection mechanisms, prominently featuring the contrastive prompt tuning introduced by Wang_2024_Advqdet, which achieved up to 99% detection rates against query-based black-box attacks. It will then transition to the 2025-2026 bifurcation in defense research: the pursuit of extreme computational efficiency versus the development of dynamic, ensemble-based systems designed to counter automated prompt injection. The section will also address strategies for securing the RLHF pipeline against poisoning and mechanistic interventions to reduce hallucinations, illustrating the ongoing co-evolutionary arms race between attackers and defenders.

outline.title: Testing Methodologies and Evaluation
outline.description: This mandatory section provides a comprehensive synthesis of the benchmarks, datasets, metrics, tools, and evaluation frameworks utilized across all LLM security threat categories. It will detail the use of domain-specific datasets, such as the MIMIC-III dataset utilized by Yang_2024_Adversarial to test healthcare vulnerabilities. The section will rigorously examine evaluation metrics, particularly the Attack Success Rate (ASR), which reached 50-71% in recent automated jailbreak studies (Zhan_2025_LLM, Wang_2025_LLM, Maloyan_2025_LLM). It will also cover the benchmarking frameworks established by Chowdhury_2024_Breaking and Li_2024_Backdoorllm for evaluating generative backdoors in models like LLaMA-2, Mistral, and GPT-J. Finally, it will critically analyze the 'LLM-as-a-judge' paradigm, referencing Friel_2023_LLM's ChainPoll methodology, to discuss the trade-offs between evaluation efficacy, computational cost, and the risk of evaluator bias.

outline.title: Discussion and Open Challenges
outline.description: This section critically analyzes the current state of LLM security research, identifying significant gaps, limitations, and future directions. It will discuss the inherent tension between model utility/alignment and security, particularly how mechanisms like RLHF can be dual-use vulnerabilities. The discussion will highlight the open challenge of securing multimodal and embodied AI systems, which present vastly larger attack surfaces than unimodal text models. It will also address the computational unsustainability of current adversarial training and dynamic ensemble defenses, calling for more efficient, mechanistically grounded security guarantees. Finally, it will explore the implications of automated, AI-driven attack generation (e.g., MCTS fuzzing, genetic algorithms) and the urgent need for proactive, rather than reactive, security paradigms.

outline.title: Conclusion
outline.description: The conclusion will synthesize the core findings of the survey, reiterating the rapid escalation of LLM security threats from 2023 to 2026. It will summarize the shift from static, isolated vulnerabilities to a complex, automated adversarial arms race encompassing poisoning, adversarial attacks, prompt injection, and hallucinations. The section will provide actionable, practical recommendations for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers, emphasizing the necessity of integrated, dynamic defense systems and rigorous, standardized testing methodologies. It will close with a forward-looking statement on the critical importance of secure-by-design principles in the next generation of foundation models.
